Subject: Post-demo: on‑prem streaming capacity & VPN/peering clarifications

Hi Tariq / Maya —

Thanks again for the call this morning. Quick recap of the perf/levers we discussed and the follow-ups we promised: 

- Business target we captured: support 250 concurrent streaming sessions (server‑side streaming, long‑lived WS) with average session throughput of ~12 tokens/sec and occasional bursts up to 60 tokens/sec.
- Latency SLO: p95 end‑to‑end token latency <= 120ms; p99 <= 300ms under normal load (no packet loss).
- Throughput: baseline 40 rps for short text gen (single-shot) and up to 55 sustained concurrent streaming connections for mixed traffic by the Dedicated cluster.

Network/ops notes needing clarification from your side:
1) How are outbound egress flows currently NATed? (single NAT gateway per AZ, autoscaling NAT, or per‑subnet NAT?)
2) IPSec vs. AWS Transit Gateway peering: do you plan to terminate tunnels at a central edge or per‑AZ?
3) Any DPI/TLS inspection appliances inline that could reassemble/terminate TCP streams? Those can add unpredictable tail latency.

Engineering ask / Redwood next steps:
- Karthik will propose a small lab validation (on‑prem VM <-> Redwood dedicated host) to emulate streaming load and packet sizes — target window 1 week.
- Ben will produce a short checklist for MTU/jumbo frame validation and suggested TCP keepalive settings.
- Please share a sample pcap of a 60s WebSocket streaming session if you can (we'll only use metadata to size packetization).

I'll loop in POA items in a follow-up with proposed dates. If any of the numbers above are off from what you intended, flag them and we'll adjust.

Thanks —
Jasmine
Jasmine Liu
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Post-demo: on‑prem streaming capacity & VPN/peering clarifications

Thanks Jasmine — useful recap. A few clarifications from our infra side: 

- NAT/egress: We use autoscaling NAT gateway per AZ behind a small fleet of NAT instances today. There is an internal LB in front; peak concurrent ephemeral flows per NAT instance is around 12k.
- Tunnels: We terminate IPSec at a central colo edge (two HA pairs), not per‑AZ. We plan to add a direct peering when the POC proves out.
- DPI: We do have a TLS inspection appliance in the core path for north‑south, but it is bypassed for certain whitelisted destinations. Not yet whitelisted Redwood.

Questions for Redwood: 
1) For the streaming SLOs, do your p95/p99 targets include time spent inside our TLS inspection appliance? If yes, we need examples of expected queueing delay to validate.
2) What are the expected packet sizes and inter‑packet timing for a 12 tokens/sec and a 60 tokens/sec stream? This will help us verify MTU fragmentation behavior.

I'll try to pull a 60s WebSocket pcap tomorrow and share (sanitized). Also attaching our rough availability windows for a lab window — can you confirm if next Tue/Wed works?

—Tariq
Tariq Singh
Sr. NetOps Lead, OrionCloud

Hi Tariq, Maya —

Appreciate the details. Quick responses inline to your questions plus a short lab plan.

- SLO scope: Our latency SLOs are measured end‑to‑end at the application layer (client -> Redwood runtime -> first token emitted). Any extra hop (TLS inspection) is counted in the p95/p99 budget unless you explicitly route the traffic around it. If you can whitelist Redwood for the POC, we can instrument to show delta.

- Packetization: Typical streaming sessions we saw in similar customers:
  * Idle keepalive packets: small (60–80 bytes) every 30s.
  * Normal streaming @12 tokens/sec: average payload frames ~400–700 bytes; inter‑packet spacing ~80–100ms.
  * Burst mode @60 tokens/sec: frames ~600–1200 bytes with inter‑packet spacing ~15–25ms.
  Note: TCP segmentation + TLS record layering can push some frames past the MTU; we recommend verifying jumbo frame support (MTU 9000) on path if you see fragmentation.

- Lab validation plan (proposed):
  1) 30m baseline: single WebSocket stream, confirm p50/p95/p99 token latency baseline.
  2) Scale step test: ramp to 250 concurrent streams over 30m, with random bursts to simulate concurrent users.
  3) IPSec tunnel eval: run identical test over your IPSec termination and with a bypass (if allowable) to compare deltas.
  4) MTU test: send controlled packet sizes to verify fragmentation behavior.

We can run the lab from Redwood's Dedicated host in us‑west and will instrument with tcpdump + application traces. For scheduling — next Tue (2026‑08‑25) 09:00–12:00 PT or Wed (2026‑08‑26) 13:00–16:00 PT are options for our infra team. Which works for you?

Ben will follow up with a short ops checklist (MTU, TCP keepalive, NAT connection tracking settings) and a minimal configuration diff you can apply.

Karthik
